column4: God joins completing His favor to the Prophet, وَيُتِمَّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكَ, with guiding him on a straight path; this states outright the section's reading of the Lord who carries a favor through to guidance.
Jacob promises that God will choose Joseph, teach him, and وَيُتِمُّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكَ, extending the completed favor to Jacob's household; the blessing is a process whose end embraces a family.
أَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِي names the favor as completed and immediately joins completion to God's approval of Islam, وَرَضِيتُ; it directly unites the section's completion and riḍā.
God makes direction toward the Sacred Mosque serve two stated ends, وَلِأُتِمَّ نِعْمَتِي عَلَيْكُمْ and guidance; this is another explicit completion-of-favor and path pairing.
After the rulings of purification, God says He intends to purify the believers and لِيُتِمَّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكُمْ; bodily preparation becomes a concrete form of favor brought to completion.
After shade, shelters, garments, and armor are enumerated, كَذَٰلِكَ يُتِمُّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكُمْ identifies the whole protective sequence as a favor completed toward submission.
مَا أَنْتَ بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ بِمَجْنُونٍ repeats the section's exact phrase and makes the Lord's favor the ground on which slander against the Prophet is denied.
فَمَا أَنْتَ بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ بِكَاهِنٍ وَلَا مَجْنُونٍ repeats the exact phrase while clearing the Prophet of two accusations; favor here includes divine vindication.
God's promise لَئِن شَكَرْتُمْ لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ makes gratitude the condition of increase, precisely realizing the source section's secondary sense “أَنْعَمَ ... زَادَ.”

Moses is returned to his mother كَيْ تَقَرَّ عَيْنُهَا وَلَا تَحْزَنَ, then rescued, tried, and brought at the appointed time; it supplies both the source's “eye's delight” sense and a long favor completed in stages.
God returns Moses to his mother so that her eye may be comforted, she may cease grieving, and she may know God's promise is true; the eye's blessing arrives as a promise carried to completion.
Solomon asks to be enabled to thank God for نِعْمَتَكَ الَّتِي أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيَّ and to do a deed تَرْضَاهُ; received favor, gratitude, family extension, and divine approval meet in one prayer.
وَمَا بِكُمْ مِنْ نِعْمَةٍ فَمِنَ اللَّهِ gives every favor a single source, grounding the section's claim that the blessing belongs to the Lord who delivers it.

The believers are told to remember being few and vulnerable before God فَآوَاكُمْ, strengthened them, and provided good things so they might thank; its shelter-to-provision sequence closely restages 93:6-8 and ends in gratitude.
وَإِنَّ لَنَا لَلْآخِرَةَ وَالْأُولَى places both the later and the first with God; it repeats 93:4's two temporal terms and opens the movement that reaches satisfaction in 92:21.
وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَى nearly answers 93:5's وَلَسَوْفَ ... فَتَرْضَى word for word; here the promised satisfaction completes the story of one who gives wealth seeking only his Lord.
فَلِلَّهِ الْآخِرَةُ وَالْأُولَى repeats the “later/first” pair and assigns both to God, preparing the following verse's statement about whom He wills and approves.
Intercession is ineffective until God permits it for one He wills and يَرْضَى; as the continuation of 53:25, approval marks the boundary within God's ownership of first and last.

The Prophet's household arrangement is said to make the women's eyes comforted, remove grief, and leave them all وَيَرْضَيْنَ بِمَا آتَيْتَهُنَّ; eye-delight, a gift received, and satisfaction converge explicitly.
God will fully pay the believers' rewards and وَيَزِيدُهُمْ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ; complete recompense followed by increase is a direct nonlexical rendering of the image's two motions.
لِيُوَفِّيَهُمْ أُجُورَهُمْ وَيَزِيدَهُمْ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ likewise places payment in full before increase from bounty, making completion open onto surplus rather than mere closure.
Those who do good receive الْحُسْنَىٰ وَزِيَادَةٌ, “the best” together with increase; the reward exceeds completion and becomes the good state named by the source's niʿmah definition.

وَيَزِيدُ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ اهْتَدَوْا هُدًى joins increase to guidance, then calls enduring good deeds better with the Lord in reward and return; increase, path, and better outcome form one movement.

كُلًّا نُمِدُّ ... مِنْ عَطَاءِ رَبِّكَ says the Lord continuously extends His gift to both groups and that His giving is not confined; it clarifies the breadth and ongoing delivery in “your Lord will give you.”
After the Lord's unrestricted giving in 17:20, this ayah says the Hereafter is greater in ranks and preference; it gives a measured parallel to the later being better than the first.
وَالْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَى repeats the section's central comparison almost exactly and adds that the better later life also remains.
“Shall I tell you of something better than that?” leads from worldly desires to gardens and رِضْوَانٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ; what is truly better culminates in abundant approval.
After lasting gardens and dwellings, وَرِضْوَانٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ أَكْبَرُ declares God's abundant approval greater; satisfaction is the surpassing completion of all listed gifts.
Paradise gives its people whatever they will, وَلَدَيْنَا مَزِيدٌ, and God still has more; fulfilled desire is followed by increase.
The garden's people have whatever they wish forever, and this is a promise charged to “your Lord”; it makes desired good a promised gift brought fully to its recipients.
God has subjected what is in the heavens and earth and أَسْبَغَ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعَمَهُ ظَاهِرَةً وَبَاطِنَةً; the verb depicts favors lavished or made ample, outward and hidden.
Abraham is شَاكِرًا لِأَنْعُمِهِ; God then chooses him and guides him to a straight path, binding gratitude for favors to selection and guidance.
As the completion of 16:121, God gives Abraham good in this world and places him among the righteous in the Hereafter; the gift spans both temporal sides rather than ending in the first.

At full maturity the servant prays to thank God for the favor given to him and his parents, to do work God approves, and to have his offspring repaired; favor is carried across a whole life and family.
God does not approve ingratitude, but وَإِنْ تَشْكُرُوا يَرْضَهُ لَكُمْ; gratitude and approval are explicitly joined, clarifying the response and endpoint of completed favor.
When the throne appears, Solomon says هَذَا مِنْ فَضْلِ رَبِّي to test whether he will thank or deny; a received marvel is read as the Lord's favor and a summons to gratitude.

At the reunion Joseph identifies the scene as the تأويل of his old dream, says his Lord made it true, brought him from prison, and gathered his family; the predicted favor has reached its end and collected his affairs.
The wall hides treasure for two orphans until they reach maturity, and the explanation says “your Lord willed” that completion as mercy; divine care shelters an orphaned good until its proper end.
God accepts Mary graciously, causes her to grow a good growth, assigns her to Zechariah, and repeatedly provides for her; child-rearing, cultivation, and provision merge in one sustained care.
God commands Jesus to remember His favor upon him and his mother, then enumerates support, teaching, miracles, and protection; it models speaking a prophetic life's completed sequence of favors.
The question “Have We not expanded your breast?” begins another divine enumeration addressed to the Prophet, continuing the form of remembered care used in 93:6-8.
“We removed from you your burden” contributes release from a former state to the neighboring enumeration of favors.
The burden “which weighed upon your back” identifies the distress repaired by 94:2, making the favor a concrete change of condition.
“We raised for you your remembrance” completes the neighboring sequence with an increased public good granted to the Prophet.
وَأَنَّهُ هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ attributes both enrichment and lasting contentment to God, directly paralleling the sufficiency granted in 93:8 and its movement toward satisfaction.
Whoever relies on God finds فَهُوَ حَسْبُهُ; God reaches His purpose and has set a measure for everything, so sufficiency is presented as care that unfailingly reaches its appointed end.
أَلَيْسَ اللَّهُ بِكَافٍ عَبْدَهُ asks whether God is not sufficient for His servant while opponents try to frighten the Prophet; divine sufficiency becomes protection amid hostile speech.
Hud tells his people to remember being made successors after Noah and being increased in stature, then to remember God's benefits; recalled favor and increase are expressly joined.
Moses tells his people اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ and recounts their rescue from Pharaoh; it models narrating a favor, and the next ayah states its increase through gratitude.

The believers are commanded to remember God's favor when hostility became brotherhood and when He rescued them from the brink of the Fire; the favor is a narrated transformation from one state to another.
وَأَحْسِنْ كَمَا أَحْسَنَ اللَّهُ إِلَيْكَ turns goodness received from God into goodness delivered onward, directly realizing the source's definition of inʿām as conveying benefit to another.

أَأَنْتُمْ تَزْرَعُونَهُ أَمْ نَحْنُ الزَّارِعُونَ assigns the crop's actual growth to God; it gives the source's dictionary image “رَبَّ الضَّيْعَةَ,” tending an estate to completion, a Quranic scene.
God revives dead land and brings grain from it for people to eat; repaired earth is carried to an edible benefit.
Gardens of palms and vines and springs opened within them develop the land-care scene begun in 36:33.
People eat the land's fruit though their hands did not make it, and are asked whether they will thank; completed cultivation reaches another as provision and calls for gratitude.
رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا uses the رب root for parents raising a small child; it is the exact child-rearing sense from which the source distinguishes the Lord's completing care.
Pharaoh's أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا uses the رب root of raising Moses as a child, furnishing the other concrete sense named in the source's opening distinction.
A benefit passed onward is pictured as a seed producing seven ears and seven hundred grains, after which God multiplies further; cultivation and increase explain how given good grows.
God expands and restricts provision, and whatever believers spend فَهُوَ يُخْلِفُهُ; good conveyed to others is met by the Provider's replacement.
People are told to rejoice in God's bounty and mercy because it is خَيْرٌ مِمَّا يَجْمَعُونَ; true delight lies in divine good rather than accumulated possessions.
God apportions livelihoods and raises people in degrees, while وَرَحْمَتُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌ مِمَّا يَجْمَعُونَ; measured worldly provision yields to the Lord's better mercy.
The Prophet is told not to stretch his eyes toward worldly bloom, for وَرِزْقُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَى; the Lord's provision is the better, enduring good.
Following 20:131, God says “We do not ask you for provision; We provide you,” and makes the final outcome belong to reverence; the source and endpoint of sufficiency are clarified.
People are commanded to remember God's favor and asked whether any creator besides God provides from heaven and earth; narration of blessing leads to its sole source.
God gives from everything people ask, and His favor cannot be counted; the completed gifts exceed any finite inventory.
وَإِنْ تَعُدُّوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ لَا تُحْصُوهَا makes divine favor uncountable, giving the section's “increase” an abundance beyond enumeration.
A person receives honor and comfort yet says رَبِّي أَكْرَمَنِ; the ayah stages the section's false reading that material expansion by itself proves divine honor.
When provision is measured tightly, the same person says رَبِّي أَهَانَنِ; alongside 89:15 it exposes the opposite but equally false equation of provision with worth.
كَلَّا rejects those readings and immediately points to failure to honor the orphan; the truth of favor is tested in whether received good is passed to the vulnerable.
Failure to urge feeding the poor continues the correction of 89:15-16 and mirrors the social obligation that follows remembered sufficiency in surah 93.
Devouring inheritance greedily shows abundance consumed rather than transmitted as good, completing the ethical diagnosis around the false claim of honor.
Excessive love of wealth identifies the attachment behind the mistaken reading of plenty as completed favor.
The addressed soul returns رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً; genuine completion ends in reciprocal satisfaction, in contrast with the unstable judgments about wealth in 89:15-16.

Pharaoh's wife calls the infant قُرَّتُ عَيْنٍ لِي وَلَكَ, although the preceding ayah says he will become an enemy and grief to Pharaoh's house; eye-delight here carries an irony that marks the limit of present perception.
بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا names preference for the nearer life as the error to which 87:17's “Hereafter is better and more lasting” responds.
The question asks whether wealth and sons supplied to deniers are being mistaken for a hastening of good things; material increase is explicitly placed under suspicion.
بَلْ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ denies that the supplied wealth is accelerated خَيْرَات, setting a boundary around what may be called true good.
After distress is removed and a favor is given, the person claims it came through personal knowledge; God calls it a trial, exposing false ownership of delivered good.
Those who count their submission as a favor to the Prophet are corrected: بَلِ اللَّهُ يَمُنُّ عَلَيْكُمْ أَنْ هَدَاكُمْ; the direction and source of favor are reversed back to God and His guidance.
يَعْرِفُونَ نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ ثُمَّ يُنْكِرُونَهَا depicts people recognizing God's favor and then denying it, the opposite of the command to tell it truthfully.
God does not change a favor He has bestowed until a people change what is in themselves; completed favor has a moral boundary and may be lost through its recipients' alteration.
Those who exchange نِعْمَتَ اللَّهِ كُفْرًا turn favor into ingratitude and lead their people to ruin; it is the destructive reversal of grateful increase in 14:7.
A secure, tranquil town receives abundant provision from every place, then denies God's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear; the full state of blessing is reversed point by point.
God says He expands provision for whom He wills and measures it, but most people do not know; expansion and restriction therefore cannot bear the honor/disgrace meanings assigned in 89:15-16.
Neither wealth nor children bring people near to God; this supplies the explicit boundary missing from the mistaken prosperity reading.
كَلَّا إِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ لَيَطْغَى warns that the human being transgresses, and the next ayah locates the trigger in imagined self-sufficiency.
أَنْ رَآهُ اسْتَغْنَى makes seeing oneself as self-sufficient a cause of rebellion, reversing 93:8's sufficiency received from God.
Qarun claims his wealth was given because of knowledge he possesses; the claim erases the giver and misreads accumulated good as self-produced.
God causes the earth to swallow Qarun and his house, and no group or self-help can save him; apparent completion in wealth proves unable to preserve itself.
The former wishers for Qarun's place now confess that God expands and restricts provision and that deniers do not prosper; the scene corrects its own false reading.
The garden owner enters his garden wronging himself and says it will never perish; he mistakes a cultivated favor for a self-securing completion.
He doubts the Hour yet assumes he would receive a better return even then; “better” is made to serve entitlement rather than God's promised later good.
His companion says he should have acknowledged “What God wills; no power except through God” upon entering; the proper speech about a garden's blessing is set against boasting.
The fruit is encompassed and the owner wrings his hands over what he spent; the finished garden becomes a ruin when treated as guaranteed possession.
Usury intended لِيَرْبُوَ in people's wealth does not increase with God, whereas alms seeking God's face are multiplied; the ayah distinguishes false increase from increase of conveyed good.
Mary is given water and ripe dates and told to eat, drink, and وَقَرِّي عَيْنًا; provision delivered in distress becomes the source section's “eye's delight.”
The servants pray for spouses and offspring as قُرَّةَ أَعْيُنٍ; the source's dictionary expression for the eye's blessing becomes a requested family good.
No soul knows what قُرَّةِ أَعْيُنٍ has been hidden as reward; the eye's blessing is both future and concealed, fitting a good whose completion lies beyond present sight.
Paradise contains what souls desire and eyes delight in; satisfaction and the source's eye-delight sense meet in an enduring good state.
Moses commands his people to remember God's favor in making among them prophets and rulers and granting what others lacked; it is communal narration of a favor unfolded through history.
The believers are told to remember God's favor and the Book and wisdom sent to instruct them; favor includes an ongoing guidance that must be recollected after receipt.
“Have you seen what you sow?” supplies the human act whose completion 56:64 assigns to God, establishing the field scene needed by the source's estate-tending dictionary form.
Rain becomes vegetation, grain, dates, grapes, olives, and pomegranates, and readers are told to look at fruit and its ripening; the scene makes beneficence visible as growth carried to maturity.
Mothers nurse for two complete years for one who wants to complete nursing, while the father must provide fairly; child-rearing is portrayed as care, provision, and an intended completion.
Recitation, prayer, and spending from God's provision are called a commerce that will not perish; it supplies the acts whose reward 35:30 is paid fully and increased.
One who wants only the immediate life receives whatever God wills and then faces Hell; it begins the contrast that 17:19-21 resolve in favor of the later gift.
One who seeks the Hereafter with faithful effort finds that effort appreciated; this identifies the recipient of the better, greater later ranks in 17:21.
God gives believers glad tidings of mercy, رِضْوَانٍ, and gardens with lasting bliss; abundant approval accompanies the completed good state.
Abraham publicly praises God for granting Ishmael and Isaac in old age; he models speaking of a long-awaited gift after it arrives.
Sheba receives two gardens, abundant provision, and the command to thank a forgiving Lord; land, delivered good, and gratitude form a completed civic blessing.
When Sheba turns away, the flood replaces the two gardens with bitter produce; the tended-land blessing is reversed through ingratitude.
After hardship is replaced by favor, a person boasts that evils have left him and becomes exultant; the transition is real but its self-satisfied reading is defective.
The patient who do good are excepted from that defective response and receive forgiveness and great reward; endurance turns changing conditions toward a lasting completion.
